angleEvaluations.reason: Clear role-reversal metaphor: the aged PHP server is drawn as caregiver and the human administrator as the frail patient. This directly inverts the expected relationship (admins repair servers) without asserting any extra factual claim beyond the article (many sites are hard to fix because versions are unsupported). The scene is simple (one large server figure, one main admin, a small queue) and reads at small print size; the single visible label 'PHP' suffices.

Object inversion is vivid: a bandage labelled as a 'patch' visibly converts into a destructive saw the moment it is applied, so the fix becomes the cause of further damage. The visual irony is strong and readable in one image, but it implicitly claims that applying patches to unsupported/old installations can actively make things worse — a causal assertion not stated in the supplied news summary.
unsupportedClaims: That applying patches to old/unsupported PHP installations actively causes additional, physical damage (i.e., the patch is harmful rather than merely ineffective).
That administrators in these affected sites are commonly applying such patches and thereby producing damage.

prompt:
Create a single editorial cartoon for English-speaking newspaper readers.
News headline (source evidence, not lettering): 10. PHP脆弱性、利用サイトの半分が修正困難 バージョン古くサポート終了（日経、日経・読売・産経・47・みんかぶ、yahoo等）2026/10/24
Satirical angle: Portray the infrastructure so obsolete that the servers have caretaking duties — a role reversal where the old PHP installation is the caregiver and the human admin is the one needing tending.
Scene: A single enormous, anthropomorphic server cabinet (its front clearly marked with one large label) sits on a stool and gently wraps a bandage around a tiny, exhausted system administrator who is slumped on its lap. The admin holds a modern laptop uselessly; a few other small admins stand in line, looking frail. The giant server is creaking and patched itself with old tape and bolts, showing age; nearby modern update tools lie unopened on the floor.
Visual turn to show in the drawing: Role reversal — before: admins are supposed to repair servers; after/revealed: the ancient server is actively nursing the fragile admin, reversing caregiver and patient roles so the infrastructure appears beyond repair.
Depict this visible ironic reversal, not a literal reenactment of the reported event or a generic portrait. The turn must read without the title. A metaphor must not assert an unreported action or guilt.
Deliver the illustration alone. The page layout adds its title separately as real text. Do not render any title, subtitle, caption, heading or footer anywhere in this image, including the white margins. Do not write any Japanese characters in the image. Do not add text beneath the figures.
Strongly reference the pen-and-ink editorial cartoon work of Georges Bigot, Charles Wirgman and Charles Keene: observant human caricature, expressive faces and gestures, lively economical contours with deliberate changes in line weight, convincing clothing folds, and sparse hand-drawn hatching. Make these nineteenth-century draughtsmen the primary visual references throughout the drawing.
Create the original artwork for a newspaper illustration that will be printed using letterpress equipment and techniques from 150 years ago, circa 1876. Draw a deliberately composed, human-looking pen-and-ink original for an engraver to turn into a relief printing block. Use economical, clearly separated lines that remain legible when printed at small column size. Deliver the clean original drawing, without simulated aged-paper or printed-ink texture. Specific recognizable characters, expressive caricature, one clear visual joke, spare composition, natural asymmetry, varied purposeful contour lines. Avoid generic AI illustration conventions, glossy perfection, decorative clutter, stock robot imagery unless the joke specifically needs it, and irrelevant objects.
Black ink strokes on pure white paper ONLY. Clear outlines; express every shadow with sparse hatching, cross-hatching or stippled marks. Leave white paper visible between strokes. No gray fills, gradients, smooth shading, color, digital painting, photorealism, artificial paper texture or engraving filter effect. Keep most areas unshaded. Compact square composition, width:height exactly 1:1, complete subjects within the frame.
Design for a small newspaper column only about 64 mm wide. Use one clear visual joke with no more than two main figures and one essential prop. Remove secondary people, inset maps, small labels and ornamental detail. Render exactly one text element in the ENTIRE image: PHP. Use bold, clean uppercase English capitals on ONE major prop. Each letter must be at least 15% of the full image height, and the word must occupy at least 30% of the image width. Make the sign physically large in the scene, never a small stamp, badge, chart, screen, speech bubble or distant billboard. If this cannot fit naturally, simplify the prop and composition to make room. No other letters, numbers or pseudo-text anywhere. Ignore ALL label or written-word instructions implicit in the headline, angle and scene except the one specified text element above. Never use fine print or tiny characters. Do NOT draw the Japanese title, a caption, a border, watermark or signature inside the image; the title will be typeset separately outside the artwork. Treat the scene as satire, and do not invent additional factual allegations beyond the supplied headline.
